posts.title: Switching off ICD shocks: ask early
posts.insight: Near the end of life an ICD can keep giving shocks that no longer help. The shock function can be switched off painlessly, without an operation, and a do-not-resuscitate decision does not do this on its own.
posts.angle: People with an ICD should know, well before the last days, that they can ask for a conversation about switching off the shocks; the Dutch and Swedish data show it often happens late or not at all.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (Swedish and Dutch device and record studies; CMAJ practice summary; UK guidance 2024) and ethical judgement (that the conversation should happen early, marked as advice)

captions.x:
Near the end of life, an implanted defibrillator (ICD) can keep giving shocks.

A Swedish hospital read the devices of 125 people after they died: 31 in 100 had been shocked in their last 24 hours. Most had their device fitted after a dangerous heart rhythm, so this figure does not apply to everyone with an ICD.

A do-not-resuscitate decision does not switch the shocks off. That needs a separate conversation and reprogramming by the heart rhythm team.

Switching off the shock function needs no operation. It is painless and can be reversed, and the pacing keeps working. It does not cause death by itself; it means a dangerous rhythm near the end of life will not be shocked.

UK heart rhythm guidance (2024) says you should have the chance to talk about this. If you have an ICD, you can raise it with your cardiology or device clinic team long before it is needed.
captions.linkedin:
Near the end of life, an implanted defibrillator (ICD) can keep giving shocks.

A Swedish hospital read the devices of 125 people after they died: 31 in 100 had received a shock in their last 24 hours of life. Most of these devices had been fitted after a previous dangerous heart rhythm, a group more likely to be shocked, so the figure should not be applied to everyone with an ICD.

A do-not-resuscitate decision does not switch the shocks off. That needs a separate conversation and reprogramming of the device by the heart rhythm team. In the same Swedish study, about 2 in 3 people who had a do-not-resuscitate order still had their shocks switched on the day before they died.

The conversation also tends to come late. In a Dutch hospital's records of 1,606 people with an ICD who died between 2006 and 2022, the shocks had been switched off beforehand for 42 in 100, and a third of those switch-offs happened on the last day of life.

What switching off involves:
1. No operation. The device is reprogrammed from outside the body.
2. It is painless and can be reversed.
3. Pacing, the part that stops the heart going too slowly, keeps working.
4. It does not cause death by itself. It means a dangerous rhythm near the end of life will not be shocked.

UK heart rhythm guidance (2024) says people with an ICD should have the chance to talk about switching off the shock function towards the end of life, and earlier UK guidance says this should usually be explained before the device is fitted.

We should offer this conversation early, when there is time to think it through. If you have an ICD, you can raise it yourself with the cardiology, heart failure or device clinic team, and a GP can help start it.

posts.title: A DNACPR decision is about CPR
posts.insight: In UK guidance a DNACPR decision covers CPR only, yet it is often read as 'do less'. Writing the CPR decision inside a whole treatment plan that lists what continues is linked with fewer harms.
posts.angle: Every treatment limit should be written alongside the care that continues; families can ask 'what will still be done?'
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (NIHR synthesis; UK nurse scenario RCT; one-hospital before-and-after; ReSPECT implementation data) and ethical judgement (that every limit should be written with the care that continues)

captions.x:
A DNACPR decision is about CPR. In UK guidance, every other treatment and all care should still be offered on its merits.

A national review of NHS practice found it was often treated as if it meant 'do not provide active treatment'.

In a UK scenario study, 231 nurses were randomly given the same deteriorating patient. With a DNACPR form, they planned fewer checks, fewer calls for help and fewer treatments. When the CPR decision was written inside a wider treatment plan, they planned the same care as with no form at all. This tested intentions, not real care.

If someone you care for has a DNACPR decision, ask the team: what will still be done?
captions.linkedin:
A DNACPR decision is about CPR. In UK guidance, every other treatment and all care should still be offered on its merits.

That is not how it is always read. A national review of NHS practice found DNACPR decisions were often treated as if they meant 'do not provide active treatment'. Staff in some studies expected fewer checks, fewer calls for senior help, and changes to pain relief and fluids.

A UK randomised scenario study tested this directly. 231 nurses were given the same deteriorating patient with a DNACPR form, with a form that set the CPR decision inside a wider treatment plan, or with no form. The DNACPR group planned fewer checks, fewer calls for help and fewer treatments. The wider-plan group planned the same care as the no-form group. It measured what nurses said they would do, not real care.

The same idea has been tried in practice. In one English hospital, replacing the stand-alone DNACPR form with a one-page plan recording the whole treatment plan was followed by fewer harmful events in patients not for CPR. That was a before-and-after study, so it shows an association rather than proof.

The ReSPECT form, used across much of the UK, records the CPR recommendation inside a wider emergency care plan. In English hospitals about 8 in 10 forms also recorded another treatment recommendation, though most still focused on CPR.

We should write every CPR decision together with a list of what continues. A decision about one treatment says nothing about a person's worth.

If someone you care for has a DNACPR decision, ask: what will still be done?

posts.title: ASPREE counted years without disability
posts.insight: ASPREE made staying alive without dementia or lasting disability its main outcome. Daily aspirin in healthy over-70s did not improve it and increased serious bleeding.
posts.angle: Prevention trials in older people should count disability-free survival alongside disease events; ASPREE shows what that reveals. Carry the secondary prevention caveat prominently.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (ASPREE results and extended follow-up; ATT secondary prevention meta-analysis) and ethical judgement (that trials should count this outcome)

captions.x:
Staying alive without dementia or lasting disability was the one main outcome of ASPREE, a trial of daily aspirin in 19,114 healthy people aged 70 and over in Australia and the USA.

Lasting disability meant being unable, or finding it very hard, to wash, dress, use the toilet or walk for at least 6 months.

Aspirin did not help. Each year about 21 in every 1000 people lost that status in both groups, and almost 10 years of follow-up showed the same. Over about 5 years, serious bleeding happened to about 4 in 100 on aspirin and 3 in 100 on dummy tablets.

This is about people who had never had a heart attack or stroke. If you take aspirin after one, keep taking it unless your doctor advises otherwise.
captions.linkedin:
Staying alive without dementia or lasting disability was the one main outcome of ASPREE, a trial of daily aspirin in 19,114 healthy people aged 70 and over (65 and over for US Black and Hispanic participants) in Australia and the USA.

Lasting disability had a concrete meaning: being unable, or finding it very hard, to do a basic daily task such as washing, dressing, using the toilet or walking, for at least 6 months.

The results:
1. Aspirin did not help people stay alive and free of dementia and disability. Each year about 21 in every 1000 people lost that status in both groups. Almost 10 years of follow-up showed the same.
2. Heart attacks, strokes and heart failure admissions were not clearly reduced.
3. Over about 5 years, serious bleeding happened to about 4 in 100 people on aspirin and about 3 in 100 on the dummy tablet.

The trial stopped early because continuing was judged futile, and by the final year only about 6 in 10 people in each group were still taking their tablets, which would dilute any effect.

An outcome defined by washing, dressing and walking tells an older person something a list of heart events alone does not. In our view, trials of preventive treatment in older people should report it alongside disease events.

One caution belongs in every retelling. ASPREE was about people who had never had a heart attack or stroke. For people who have, trials show aspirin prevents further ones. If you take aspirin after a heart attack or stroke, keep taking it unless your doctor advises otherwise.

posts.title: No upper age for the 999 call
posts.insight: Clot-busting stroke treatment was tested in many people over 80 and helped them, with a real bleeding risk; eligibility depends on time and a brain scan, not age. Call 999 at once at any age.
posts.angle: Age alone should never be the reason an older person is not assessed for emergency stroke treatment; state the bleeding risk as plainly as the benefit.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (IST-3 enrolment; 9-trial individual patient meta-analysis; ESO guideline) and clinical interpretation (the 999 instruction follows from time dependence) with ethical judgement on age

captions.x:
Stroke symptoms at 85 need the same immediate 999 call as stroke symptoms at 55.

Early trials of the clot-busting drug alteplase included few people over 80. Then IST-3 enrolled 3035 people, and 1617 of them (53 in 100) were over 80.

Pooling 9 trials, among 1729 people over 80, about 18 in 100 given the drug had no significant disability 3 to 6 months later, against 13 in 100 without it.

The risk is real. Across all ages, about 3 in 100 treated people had a fatal brain bleed within a week, against fewer than 1 in 100 untreated.

Whether treatment is possible depends on how long ago the stroke started and a brain scan, and it helps more the sooner it is given. European guideline authors agreed that age alone should not be a reason to withhold it.

So call 999 straight away, whatever the person's age.
captions.linkedin:
Stroke symptoms at 85 need the same immediate 999 call as stroke symptoms at 55.

For years, older people were largely missing from the evidence. The IST-3 authors reported that before their trial, trials of the clot-busting drug alteplase had included only 79 people over 80, and the drug was first licensed in Europe only for people under 80.

IST-3 changed that. It enrolled 3035 people, and 1617 of them (53 in 100) were over 80. About half received the drug and half did not.

The clearest answer for older people comes from a combined analysis of 9 trials, which included 1729 people over 80. About 18 in 100 of those given the drug were left with no significant disability 3 to 6 months later, compared with about 13 in 100 who did not get it. The relative benefit was similar to that in younger people. IST-3's own main outcome did not show a clear difference on its own.

The harm is as real as the benefit. Across all ages, about 3 in 100 people given the drug had a fatal bleed in the brain within a week, compared with fewer than 1 in 100 without it.

Time changes the balance. Within 3 hours, 33 in 100 treated people had no significant disability afterwards, against 23 in 100 untreated. Whether treatment is possible depends on how long ago the stroke started, a brain scan to rule out bleeding, and other criteria.

European stroke guidelines strongly recommend this treatment for people over 80 whose stroke started less than 4.5 hours ago, when other criteria are met. All nine members of the guideline group agreed that age alone should not be a reason to withhold it.

Call 999 straight away for stroke symptoms, whatever the person's age.

posts.title: A geriatric assessment before cancer treatment
posts.insight: In a US trial of people aged 70 and over starting cancer treatment, giving the oncology team a geriatric assessment with recommendations cut serious side effects from 71 to 51 in 100, with similar survival.
posts.angle: Older people starting chemotherapy should have a geriatric assessment, as ASCO recommends; in the UK it is often unavailable, so families can ask.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (GAP70+ and GAIN trials; ASCO guideline; UK SIOG review) and clinical/ethical judgement (that people should have it and can ask)

captions.x:
Before cancer treatment at 70 or over, a check of daily function, falls, memory, mood, nutrition, medicines and support at home can change the plan.

In a US trial of 718 people aged 70 and over starting treatment for cancer that could not be cured, some cancer teams were given this geriatric assessment with advice on each problem. Over 3 months, serious side effects happened to about 51 in 100 of their patients, against 71 in 100 with usual care.

Those teams more often started at a lower dose, and fewer people fell (12 vs 21 in 100). Survival was similar at 6 months and 1 year, though the trial was not designed to test that.

US cancer guidance recommends this assessment for everyone over 65 with cancer. UK specialists report that few patients can get it from a specialist team. You can ask the cancer team whether it is possible.
captions.linkedin:
Before cancer treatment at 70 or over, a check of daily function, falls, memory, mood, nutrition, medicines and support at home can change the plan.

That check is a geriatric assessment. In the GAP70+ trial, 718 people aged 70 and over (average age 77) were starting treatment for cancer that could not be cured, in US community cancer practices. Some cancer teams were given each person's assessment with advice on what to do about each problem. The others gave usual care.

Over the next 3 months, serious side effects (grade 3 to 5, which includes hospital-level problems) happened to about 51 in 100 people whose team had the assessment, against 71 in 100 whose team did not.

The assessment changed what teams did. They more often started with a lower dose (about 49 in 100 vs 35 in 100). Fewer people fell over 3 months (about 12 in 100 vs 21 in 100), and a few more medicines were stopped.

Survival was similar: about 72 in 100 vs 75 in 100 alive at 6 months, a difference that could be chance, and similar at 1 year. The trial was not designed to show that survival was unaffected.

A second US trial, of 605 people aged 65 and over starting chemotherapy, found serious side effects in about 51 in 100 with a specialist team acting on the assessment, against 61 in 100 without. It did not show clear differences in hospital admissions or survival.

The American Society of Clinical Oncology recommends a geriatric assessment for everyone over 65 with cancer. In the UK, specialists in older people's cancer care reported in 2024 that only a small proportion of patients can get this from a specialist team.

If you or a relative are starting cancer treatment, it is reasonable to ask the cancer team whether an assessment of function, memory, medicines and support, or a referral to an older people's specialist, is possible.

posts.title: How many days will this treatment take?
posts.insight: Cancer researchers now count 'contact days', days spent going somewhere for health care. Older people with advanced cancer in US trials spent nearly 1 day in 5 this way in their first year; treatment can also give days back.
posts.angle: Older people are entitled to know how many days a treatment is likely to take, and what it may give back, before agreeing.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (CO.17 secondary analysis; Gupta 2025 SWOG analysis; Mexican cohort) and ethical judgement (entitlement to this information)

captions.x:
Some cancer researchers count a one-hour blood test as a whole day. They call these contact days: any day you have to go somewhere for health care.

In US cancer trials, people aged 65 and over with advanced cancer spent a median of 48 contact days in their first year, nearly 1 day in 5.

The count leaves out the family member who drives, waits and sits with you.

Days taken are one side of the decision. In one cancer trial (median age 63), people whose cancer responded spent more contact days on treatment (41 vs 10) but also had more days at home (186 vs 132).

Before agreeing to a treatment, you can ask: how many days is this likely to take, and what might it give back?
captions.linkedin:
Some cancer researchers count a one-hour blood test as a whole day. They call these contact days: any day a person has to go somewhere for health care, whether for a blood test, a scan, a drip, an emergency visit or a night in hospital.

The numbers are large for older people. In US cancer trials, people aged 65 and over with advanced cancer spent a median of 48 days in contact with health services in their first year, nearly 1 day in every 5. A study of older people having palliative cancer treatment in Mexico found a similar share.

The count still leaves things out. It does not include the time family members spend driving, waiting and sitting with the person, or the travel and waiting itself. The cost of a treatment day is often shared.

This is not an argument against treatment. In the CO.17 trial, where people chose between weekly drip treatment and supportive care alone (median age 63), the treated group spent a median of 28 contact days against 10. But people whose cancer responded to treatment spent more days in contact (41 vs 10) and also had more days at home (186 vs 132). Days taken are one side of the decision; days given back are the other.

Questions you can ask before agreeing to a treatment:
1. How many days a month is this likely to take, counting tests and check-ups?
2. How far will I travel, and who needs to come with me?
3. What is it likely to give back, in time at home or in how I feel?

In our view, clinicians should offer this information when discussing options, and older people should feel free to ask for it.

posts.title: QRISK above 10% after 75 settles nothing
posts.insight: By about 75 even ideal risk factors push QRISK past 10%, and QRISK3 separates older people's risks poorly. STAREE now shows statins in healthy over-70s cut cardiovascular events without clearly improving disability-free survival.
posts.angle: After 75, a QRISK result above 10% should open the statin conversation; the decision rests on what the person wants to prevent, time to benefit, other illnesses, frailty and preference.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (Ueda 2017 QRISK2 analysis; Livingstone 2021 QRISK3 performance; STAREE 2026; Yourman 2021 time to benefit) and clinical interpretation (what the conversation should cover)

captions.x:
By about 75, the QRISK calculator puts almost everyone above the 10% statin line, even people with ideal numbers.

In a 2017 analysis with QRISK2, a never-smoker of healthy weight with systolic 110 and a good cholesterol ratio crossed 10% between 60 and 70 (men) or 65 and 75 (women). In an English survey sample aged 75 to 84 without heart disease, every one was above it.

In 2.9 million UK records, QRISK3 was poor at separating who would have an event at 65 and over, and it overestimated risk.

STAREE (NEJM, August 2026; 9971 Australians aged 70+, no diabetes or dementia): a statin cut major cardiovascular events from about 8 to 6 in 100 over 6 years, but did not clearly change staying alive without dementia or disability.

So after 75 a result above 10% opens the conversation. The decision rests on what the person wants to prevent, time to benefit, other illnesses, frailty and preference.
captions.linkedin:
By about 75, the QRISK calculator puts almost everyone above the 10% statin line, even people with ideal numbers.

The calculator gives great weight to age. In a 2017 analysis using QRISK2 (the version in use when the 10% threshold was set), a never-smoker of healthy weight with a systolic of 110 and a good cholesterol ratio went above 10% between 60 and 70 for men and between 65 and 75 for women. In a survey sample of English adults aged 75 to 84 without heart disease, every one was above it.

The newer version does not rescue the threshold. In UK GP records of 2.9 million people, QRISK3 worked well in younger adults. At 65 and over it was poor at telling apart who would and would not have a heart attack or stroke, and it overestimated risk, more so once deaths from other causes were counted. About 1 in 5 people aged 75 to 84 died of something else during follow-up.

We now have direct trial evidence. STAREE (NEJM, August 2026) gave 9971 Australians aged 70 and over (average 75), without heart disease, stroke, diabetes or dementia, a statin or a dummy tablet. Over about 6 years:
1. About 6 in 100 on the statin and 8 in 100 on the dummy tablet had a heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death or a procedure to open a heart artery.
2. Staying alive without dementia or lasting disability did not clearly change (about 13 vs 14 in 100 lost it).
These are crude proportions from the abstract; results for the over-75s and the size of side effects were not in it.

Time to benefit also counts. In trials of people aged 50 to 75, it took about 2.5 years of treating 100 people to prevent one event, and those people were younger than most over-75s.

So after 75, a QRISK result above 10% opens the statin conversation. The decision rests on what the person wants to prevent, how long benefit takes, other illnesses, frailty and their preference.

posts.title: Blood pressure after 75: read who the trial left out
posts.insight: SPRINT showed benefit from intensive blood pressure lowering in over-75s well enough to join, but excluded care home residents, people with dementia, diabetes, stroke or a big standing drop. For them the target is an extrapolation; standing pressure, falls and goals should guide treatment.
posts.angle: Guide blood pressure treatment in older people by standing blood pressure, falls, symptoms and goals as well as targets; do not withhold treatment from fit older people, in whom benefit was shown.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (SPRINT over-75 analysis; Drawz 2020; Juraschek 2023; Tinetti 2014, association only; NG136 summary) and clinical interpretation (how to apply this to people outside the trial)

captions.x:
Standing blood pressure, falls, symptoms and the person's goals should guide blood pressure treatment in an older person, as well as any target.

SPRINT, the trial behind US and European targets, showed benefit in 2636 people aged 75 and over: aiming below 120 systolic rather than 140 meant fewer cardiovascular events (about 2.6 vs 3.9 in 100 a year), with serious adverse events similar (about 48 in 100 in each group). About 3 in 10 were classed as frail, and benefit looked similar in them.

It did not enrol people in care homes, with dementia, diabetes or previous stroke, expected to live under 3 years, or whose systolic fell below 110 after a minute standing. Its readings were unattended automated averages; routine clinic readings ran about 5 to 7 mmHg higher.

UK guidance: measure standing pressure at 80 and over, in type 2 diabetes and with postural dizziness, and judge treatment on the standing reading if systolic falls by more than 20.

Over-75s well enough to join the trial gained from treatment. For people it left out, its target is an extrapolation that needs judgement.
captions.linkedin:
Standing blood pressure, falls, symptoms and the person's goals should guide blood pressure treatment in an older person, as well as any target.

Start with what the evidence shows. SPRINT, the trial behind the lower targets in the 2017 US and 2018 European guidelines, included 2636 people aged 75 and over (average age 80). Aiming for a systolic below 120 rather than below 140 meant fewer heart attacks, strokes, heart failure admissions and cardiovascular deaths: about 2.6 vs 3.9 in 100 each year. Over about 3 years, one event was prevented for every 27 people treated this way. Serious adverse events were equally common (about 48 in 100 in each group), and injurious falls did not differ clearly. About 3 in 10 counted as frail on a frailty index, and benefit looked similar in them, in an exploratory analysis.

Then read who it left out. SPRINT did not enrol people living in care homes, people with dementia, diabetes or a previous stroke, people expected to live less than 3 years, or people whose systolic fell below 110 after a minute of standing. Its own authors wrote that the results do not tell us the right target for people in care homes or with diabetes, stroke or heart failure.

Two measurement points:
1. SPRINT averaged 3 automated readings after 5 minutes' rest with no staff in the room. Routine clinic readings in the same people averaged about 5 to 7 mmHg higher, and the gap varied widely.
2. UK guidance (NG136) asks for a standing reading at 80 and over, in type 2 diabetes and with postural dizziness, and to judge treatment on the standing reading if systolic falls by more than 20. NICE did not adopt the SPRINT targets.

The evidence on postural drops pulls both ways. Across 9 trials, lowering pressure helped people with a drop on standing as much as those without. In older people outside trials, taking blood pressure tablets was linked with more serious fall injuries, especially after a previous injurious fall; that study does not show the tablets caused the falls.

My reading: treat over-75s who resemble the trial population, and for people the trial left out, treat to the standing reading, their falls and their goals.

posts.title: Dialysis or conservative kidney care
posts.insight: NICE says people whose kidneys are failing should be offered dialysis or conservative kidney care and decide jointly, yet UK leaflets often present dialysis as the default. In older US veterans, starting dialysis early made little clear difference to survival and cost about 2 weeks at home.
posts.angle: A real choice with trade-offs in both directions: take questions about time at home, travel, hospital and symptoms to the kidney team.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (NICE NG107 via Renal Association commentary; Sowden 2025; Montez-Rath 2024; Kurella Tamura 2009) and ethical judgement (that both options should be discussed fully)

captions.x:
NICE says people whose kidneys are likely to fail should be offered a choice: dialysis (or a transplant), or conservative kidney care, decided together with them.

Conservative kidney care is planned, active care without dialysis: treating symptoms, protecting the kidney function that is left, and planning ahead.

Yet a study of leaflets from four UK kidney units found dialysis presented as the expected choice, with conservative care often left out.

No randomised trial has compared the two. In about 20,000 US veterans aged 65 and over, starting dialysis as soon as kidney function fell very low made little clear difference to survival over 3 years, and meant about 2 weeks fewer days at home. Compared with never having dialysis, it added about 11 weeks of life, still with about 2 weeks fewer at home.

Questions for the kidney team: what would each option mean for time at home, travel, hospital visits and symptoms? What would conservative care involve here?
captions.linkedin:
NICE says people whose kidneys are likely to fail should be offered a choice: dialysis (or a transplant), or conservative kidney care. The decision should be made with them, and planning should start about a year ahead.

Conservative kidney care is planned, active care without dialysis. The kidney team treats symptoms, tries to protect the kidney function that is left, and helps with planning ahead. People choosing it should be offered the same full assessment by a kidney dietitian as people starting dialysis.

The choice is not always presented evenly. A study of patient leaflets from four UK kidney units found that dialysis was presented as the expected choice. Conservative care was often left out, and when it was mentioned it came last and was described negatively.

What the evidence shows, and its limits:
1. No randomised trial has compared dialysis with conservative care, and comparative evidence is weak.
2. In a large US study of about 20,000 veterans aged 65 and over (average age 78), starting dialysis as soon as kidney function fell very low made little clear difference to survival over 3 years, and meant about 2 weeks fewer days at home rather than in hospital or a care home. Compared with never having dialysis, it added about 11 weeks of life but still meant about 2 weeks fewer at home. Nearly all were men.
3. Among US nursing home residents who started dialysis in 1998 to 2000, a year later 58 in 100 had died and only 13 in 100 were as able to look after themselves as before. There was no comparison group without dialysis, so this does not show what conservative care would have done.

Studies disagree on who gains most from dialysis, so the choice depends on the person as much as on the numbers.

Questions to take to the kidney team: what would each option mean for time at home, travel, hospital visits and symptoms? How many sessions a week, and how far would I travel? What would conservative care involve here?

More posts in the Weighing it up series take one treatment decision at a time.

posts.title: Ask what a normal day looks like at three months
posts.insight: After planned major abdominal surgery in people over 60, basic self-care took about 3 months to recover on average and household tasks about 6, and some never fully recovered. It is a fair question to ask before agreeing.
posts.angle: Before a major operation, ask what a normal day is likely to look like at three months; many older people weigh loss of independence heavily, and UK consent law covers risks significant to you.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (Lawrence 2004 cohort; Fried 2002 preferences study) and legal/ethical judgement (Montgomery test; the argument that loss of daily function is such a risk is marked as the author's view)

captions.x:
What will a normal day look like three months after a major operation?

It is a fair question to put to a surgical team. In a US study of 372 people aged 60 and over having planned major abdominal operations, getting back to usual washing and dressing took about 3 months on average. Household tasks and getting out took about 6. At 6 months, about 1 in 10 had not recovered their basic daily activities.

Many older people weigh independence heavily. In a US study of 226 seriously ill people aged 60 and over, about 3 in 4 said they would not choose a treatment that left them with severe physical disability.

UK consent law asks doctors to tell you about risks a reasonable person in your position would think significant. In my view, not getting back to washing, dressing or living at home is such a risk.

You can also ask: what is the best case, the worst case and the most likely?
captions.linkedin:
What will a normal day look like three months after a major operation?

It is a fair question to put to a surgical team, and the answer may shape the decision as much as the list of complications.

Recovery of everyday life can take months. In a US study of 372 people aged 60 and over having planned major abdominal operations (average age 69), it took on average about 3 months to get back to their usual level of basic daily activities such as washing and dressing. Household tasks and getting out, such as shopping, cooking and managing money, took about 6 months. At 6 months, about 1 in 10 had not recovered their basic daily activities and about 1 in 5 their household activities. That study is from 2004, before enhanced recovery became widespread, and averages hide wide variation.

Many older people weigh independence heavily. In a US study of 226 seriously ill people aged 60 and over, almost all would accept a simple treatment that kept them as they were. About 3 in 4 said they would not choose it if it left them alive with severe physical disability, and about 9 in 10 if it left them with severe problems with thinking and memory.

Since the 2015 Montgomery ruling, UK doctors must tell you about any risk a reasonable person in your position would think significant, or that they know is significant to you, and about reasonable alternatives. In my view, not getting back to washing, dressing or living at home is that kind of risk for many older people.

Questions you can ask:
1. What is a normal day likely to look like at three months?
2. What is the best case, the worst case and the most likely outcome?
3. What are the alternatives, and what would each mean for daily life?

posts.title: How to talk about stopping screening
posts.insight: Older adults in US studies were often open to stopping cancer screening, but disliked being told they might not live long enough to benefit; they preferred explanations about their other health priorities, and liked no explanation least.
posts.angle: When advising an older person to stop screening, explain it by benefit, harm and their other priorities, and offer prognosis to those who want it.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (Schoenborn 2017 interviews; Schoenborn 2018 survey) and clinical/ethical judgement (how to phrase the advice, marked as such)

posts.title: Setting up a time-limited trial
posts.insight: A time-limited trial is an agreed plan to give a treatment for a set time, with named signs of response and a review with options to continue, stop and focus on comfort, or extend. The plan is often incomplete in practice.
posts.angle: When benefit is uncertain, offer a time-limited trial with written signs, a duration and a review, agreed with the person or family.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical (ATS 2024 consensus definition; Chang 2021 before-and-after; Kruser 2024; Piscitello 2025) and clinical judgement (applying it beyond critical care is extrapolation, and the rationale is not a measured effect)

captions.x:
When nobody knows whether a treatment will help, a time-limited trial gives it a fair chance with an agreed review.

Expert consensus (ATS 2024) sets out the core. The plan is offered to the person or family, who can agree to it. It names the treatment, how long it runs, the signs that would show it is working or not, and what happens at review: carry on, stop and focus on comfort, or extend.

In a US before-and-after study in three intensive care units (mean age 64), after doctors were trained in this approach, family meetings named signs of improvement in almost 9 in 10 cases, up from about 1 in 5. Median ICU stay fell from 8.7 to 7.4 days; hospital deaths were unchanged (58 in 100).

Reviews find parts of the plan are often missing. Write down the signs, the date and the plan for either result.
captions.linkedin:
When nobody knows whether a treatment will help, a time-limited trial gives it a fair chance with an agreed review.

The definition comes from expert consensus (American Thoracic Society, 2024): an agreed plan to give a treatment for a set time, after which the person's response guides the next step. That step can be to carry on, to stop and focus on comfort, or to extend the trial.

What separates it from 'let's see how it goes':
1. The plan is offered to the person or family, who can agree to it.
2. It names the treatment and how long it will run.
3. It names the signs that would show it is working or not.
4. It says what happens at the review.
These are core items from a fuller consensus of 16 elements, and the plan can be extended rather than binding.

The stated aim is a middle path between open-ended treatment and stopping at once: full-quality care for a fair period, judged by criteria agreed in advance. That is the rationale, not a measured result.

What has been measured is modest. In a US before-and-after study in three intensive care units (not specific to older people, mean age 64), training doctors to use time-limited trials raised the share of family meetings that named signs of improvement from about 1 in 5 to almost 9 in 10. Median ICU stay fell from 8.7 to 7.4 days, and fewer people were ventilated (86 vs 73 in 100). Hospital deaths did not change (58 in 100 in both periods).

In practice the approach is often done partly. Reviews find parts of the plan missing, and in one US health system only about 1 in 100 goals-of-care notes recorded a time-limited trial.

The consensus was written for critical care; using it for other decisions in older people is a reasonable extrapolation. Write down the signs, the date and the plan for either result.
